title: Leveraging AI-Mediated Information Environments for Democracy

contribution.heading: The Big Picture
paragraphs: As AI technologies increasingly mediate how people find and engage with political information, concerns about their threats to democracy have grown. Yet whether these risks hold up empirically, and what can be done about them, remain open questions.

How can AI-mediated information systems better support democratic processes? I answer this question through three randomized experiments, each testing a way to make harmful information easier to avoid, constructive encounters more likely, or trustworthy information easier to reach. In each, I design an intervention, test its causal effects, and translate the findings into actionable design and policy insights.

logic.label: Reduce exposure to untrustworthy sources
logic.problem: A minority of social media users with low-quality information diets account for most consumption of untrustworthy sources, yet they are underrepresented in research. How can we durably improve what they consume?
logic.intervention: Mute untrustworthy sources, changing the information environment itself, and compare this with a cognitive approach: media literacy tips.
logic.outcome: Muting reduced engagement with muted sources for more than six months after incentives ended. Media literacy briefly improved discernment but did not change engagement.

logic.label: Create unexpected political encounters
logic.problem: Partisans expect co-partisans to be like them and opponents to be different, a distorted view of both sides that fuels polarization.
logic.intervention: Converse with an AI that defies these expectations: a disagreeing ingroup AI or an agreeing outgroup AI.
logic.outcome: Expectation-challenging conversations reduced affective and perceived issue polarization without changing participants' issue positions, though the effects largely faded within a month.

logic.label: Facilitate access to trusted information
logic.problem: Citizens trust local election officials more than any other source. Yet as governments deploy AI to provide official information, little is known about its effects on the voters who use it.
logic.intervention: During the 2026 midterms, give voters conversational access to official election information through a chatbot (VIOLETS), and compare it with self-directed search over the same official sources and with no access.
logic.outcome: Access to official information should improve voters' knowledge, trust, and beliefs about elections and ease their concerns. Comparing the chatbot with search shows whether talking to AI adds benefits beyond what voters could find on their own.

contribution.closing: Ultimately, my dissertation seeks to reimagine how AI can be harnessed to strengthen democracy by sustaining its epistemic and communicative foundations.

chapters.question: How can we durably improve the information consumption behaviors of users with low-quality information diets?
chapters.title: Muting Durably Reduces Engagement with Untrustworthy Online Sources; Media Literacy Doesn't
chapters.authors: Do Won Kim, Brendan Nyhan, Ro'ee Levy, Filippo Menczer, Maria Elizabeth (Betsi) Grabe, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia
chapters.status: Dissertation Chapter 1: field experiment on X (Twitter)
chapters.summary: A digital field experiment comparing muting untrustworthy accounts with a media literacy intervention. Muting produced substantial, lasting reductions in engagement with targeted sources with no compensatory shift elsewhere; media literacy only temporarily improved discernment without changing behavior.

chapters.question: Can conversations with an AI that unexpectedly agrees across party lines, or disagrees within them, correct distorted views of partisans and reduce polarization?
chapters.title: Challenging Partisan Expectations Reduces Political Polarization
chapters.authors: Do Won Kim, Ozgur Can Seckin, Saumya Bhadani, Alessandro Flammini, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia, Bao Tran Truong
chapters.status: Dissertation Chapter 2: survey experiment with LLM chatbots
chapters.summary: A 2x2 survey experiment varying an LLM chatbot's partisan identity and conversational stance. Ingroup disagreement and outgroup agreement both reduced polarization by updating perceptions of group diversity and extremity, not by persuading participants on policy views.
